items.caption:
Born blind, they still dream. Just with fewer pictures.
In a 2014 study (11 blind from birth, 14 late blind, 25 sighted), the blind-from-birth reported fewer visual and more sound, touch, taste and smell impressions, and more nightmares (about 25% of dreams vs about 6%). Why is a hypothesis.

items.hypothesis: Variant vs 1008-1 (control): the only change is hook type, a question addressed to the viewer ('Does a scary film before bed change your dreams?', 48 characters) instead of a statement (55 characters). Same series, split scene, night theme, 6 slides, payoff on slide 2, caption structure. Expected: higher watched-full % than the control. Topics differ but share the family: what shapes dream content.
items.caption:
Does a scary film before bed change your dreams?
In a 2016 survey of 1,287 people (ages 10 to 60, in Turkey), those who reported violent media within 90 minutes of bed were about 13 times more likely to report a violent dream that night. It is a link, not proof of cause.

items.caption:
Do octopuses dream?
In lab studies, octopuses have a quiet sleep plus short bouts of "active sleep" in which skin patterns change fast and brain activity resembles waking (Nature, 2023; an earlier iScience 2021 study saw the same two states). Whether that is dreaming is still unknown; replaying the day is one idea.
